User’s parents have lived with them in the U.S. for about nine months, help with household work/cooking/English classes, and are not currently working. It is not yet established that they have actually overstayed: a B-2 visitor’s admitted period may have been shortened or extended, and the exact I-94/visa facts must be checked. Do not assume an overstay or other violation from length of residence alone. Their immigration history, authorized stay, prior status, work, public benefits, and entries/exits are relevant.

For possible inadmissibility, accurately distinguish unlawful presence from an immigration violation. Unlawful-presence accrual generally begins after a status violation under INA 105(a), and the 180-day/one-year rules for certain waivers involve specific status and departure circumstances; a nine-month stay does not automatically establish a nine-month unlawful-presence period. A short unlawful presence may fall within INA 212(g) 30-day/180-day grounds and generally is not waived by I-601/I-601A. I-601A provisional waiver eligibility and nexus to an immediate relative U.S. citizen/LPR petition are narrow and should not be assumed. Other grounds and waivers (for example I-212) may require separate analysis.

trajectory:
User is considering applying for a U.S. green card but has not specified the immigration category, current immigration status, whether the parents are U.S. citizens/LPRs, or whether they are immigrating with the user. They asked for an overview of eligibility, required forms/documents, timeline, common mistakes, and what happens after submitting a petition and supporting documents. They are especially concerned about financial sponsorship and whether nonworking parents living with them should be included in financial calculations.

User’s parents have lived with them in the U.S. for the past six months. They help with household chores, cooking, and English-language classes, and the family has enjoyed having them there. The user said their parents are currently not working and are living with them; clarify whether the user fully supports them, whether they have separate income/assets, and whether they have valid immigration status. Their immigration history, possible unauthorized stay, receipt of public benefits, and whether they are included as applicants may be relevant to immigration strategy, but do not assume negative impact merely because they live together.

For financial questions, distinguish between: (1) the petitioner/sponsor completing Form I-864, if required by the applicant’s category; and (2) the principal applicant’s own adjustment application and public-charge evidence. A household member’s presence does not automatically require the user to claim the parents on an I-864 unless the parents are the qualifying immigrants/dependents under the form’s instructions. The user should provide accurate information about their household, income, assets, expenses, tax returns, and any benefits or support received. The previous advice suggesting that parents’ expenses must automatically be counted under the I-864 may be too broad; exact treatment depends on the filing category, household definition, and the parents’ immigration/financial circumstances. Recommend checking current USCIS instructions or consulting a qualified immigration attorney.
